activity.name: mcp__gello__add_question
activity.arg:
## How should the palette's keyboard shortcuts resolve the format's letter collisions?

Criterion 5 asks for "a keyboard shortcut matching its letter in the file
format". The format reuses its letters across the three axes, so a bare letter
key cannot name one entry:

| letter | block type | behaviour | trigger type |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A` | Simple | SittingDuck | Start |
| `B` | Hardling | Spinner | Stop |
| `C` | Concrete | Vanisher | StartStop |
| `D` | SimpleTop | Repulsor | — |
| `E`–`I` | — | Evaders, Portal | — |
| `R`, `S` | — | — | the two receivers |
| `Z` | Obstacle | — | — |

The token resolves this by *position* (1st char is the type, 2nd the behaviour,
3rd the trigger); a keyboard has no positions. Trigger group is `0`–`9` and
collides with nothing either way.

Which do you want?

- [ ] **A — one modifier per axis.** Bare `A`–`D`/`Z` set the block type, `Shift`+`A`–`I` set the behaviour, `Alt`+`A`/`B`/`C`/`R`/`S` set the trigger type, `0`–`9` set the group. Non-modal: every entry is one press, always, and the block type — the thing you change most — keeps the bare letter. (`Alt` rather than `Ctrl` so that `c0011`'s `Ctrl+Z` undo and `c0012`'s `Ctrl+S` save do not later collide with trigger `Z`… `S`.)
- [ ] **B — type the token.** Press `A` `A` and you have typed `AA`; a third and fourth press add the trigger and its group. Matches the file format exactly, and nothing needs a modifier — but it is modal, and changing *just* the behaviour of the current brush means retyping the type first.
- [ ] **C — bare letters, one axis wins each.** `A`–`D` and `Z` go to the block type, `E`–`I` to the behaviour, `R`/`S` to the trigger receivers, `0`–`9` to the group; the colliding behaviours (SittingDuck…Repulsor) and triggers (Start/Stop/StartStop) are then click-only, with no shortcut. Simplest to use, but leaves the most common behaviour of all — `A`, SittingDuck — unreachable from the keyboard, so criterion 5 is only partly met.
- [ ] Something else (say what)

My recommendation is **A**: it is the only one that gives every entry its own
one-press shortcut without a mode, and the modifier still "matches the letter"
the format uses.

activity.name: Bash
activity.arg:
git add src/editor/settings.rs src/editor/mod.rs && git commit -F - <<'MSG'
c0010: a level is more than its grid

Nine rows in a panel top left - background, scroll speed, balls at once, win
percentage, time limit, extra balls, grabbers and the two side walls. Everything
in `LevelDefinition` except the `targets` the grid editor already owns and the
free-floating `obstacles` the epic put out of scope.

Every setting is a stepper: a label, the value, and a `<` and a `>` that walk it.
There is no text entry anywhere in this game to type a number into, and a stepper
needs none - it also means no setting can be left holding an invalid value,
because the step is what keeps it in range. That made `time_limit` cheap enough
to include after all, so it is in, with `None` sitting one rung below the
shortest limit. What a *file* holds is still anything at all, so the panel shows
whatever is in one - `-5` balls, a 500% win criterion, a `NaN` scroll speed - and
the first click snaps it back onto the ladder instead of carrying it along.

The ends of the ranges are where the rest of the game puts them.
Scroll velocity stops at 0 because `arena_update_background` only wraps a segment
that has run off the near end, so a negative one sends the backdrop away and
never brings it back. Balls at once starts at 1 because `MatchEvent::BallSpawn`
only adds a ball while `balls_in_play` is under it, so 0 is a level that can
never be launched. The win percentage covers all of 0-100%: it is the fraction of
blocks hit rather than lost, so 0% is a meaningful "clear the level, however
badly".

Backgrounds are a named list rather than free text. `BACKGROUNDS` holds the four
scenes the levels use; offering every scene in `ship3_003.glb` would offer the
ball and the paddle as backdrops. A level naming one the panel has never heard of
is still shown - stepping it joins the list at the end it was stepped from,
rather than jumping into the middle of it.

The two pickup rows count pickups, not the amounts they carry. The panel adds a
`MoreBalls(1)` or a `Grabber(1)` and takes back the last of that kind, so a level
that hand-authored a `MoreBalls(3)` keeps it and gains and loses whole pickups
either side of it; the amounts are read nowhere in the game today. `Grabber` is
constructed for the first time here, which is what the card wanted the row for.

The panel hit-tests its own rectangles rather than going through `Interaction`,
for the reason `c0009` worked out first: Bevy 0.19's `ui_focus_system` needs the
whole UI stack, which a headless test app cannot stand up. `settings_rows()` is
both what is drawn and what a click is read against, so the two cannot drift -
the same trade the grid already makes with `world_to_cell` rather than mesh
picking. A press rather than a hold, because a stepper walked once a frame runs
its whole range in a fifth of a second.

A click on the panel is also not a click on the play field. `cell_under_cursor`
hands back no cell for a pointer inside `panel_rect()`, which takes the highlight
with it - the alternative is a covered cell sitting under the panel still looking
armed. On the game's own 1600x800 window the panel is clear of even the widest
shipped level, but the camera keeps the field on screen at any aspect ratio, and
a tall narrow window puts the far corner of a 9-wide grid behind it. That is the
window the test uses.

25 new tests, 157 green, build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
